---
title: "Concepts"
subtitle: "Learnings and issues, weights, scopes, and the git-native store."
---

## The base skill is the architecture; Whetstone is the weights

> A skill is the **architecture** — shared, tested, canonical, the same for everyone. Whetstone is
> the **weights** — everything learned about *your* preferences, layered on at runtime and never
> baked into the skill.

Whetstone never modifies the skill. It keeps a separate, per-skill memory and applies it at the
start of each run, so your taste can evolve — and even run against the skill's defaults — without
mutating something everyone shares.

## Learnings vs. issues

Every entry Whetstone stores has a **polarity**:

```{=html}
<div class="ws-cards" style="margin-top:1.25rem;">
  <div class="ws-card">
    <div class="ws-card-icon">≈</div>
    <h3 class="ws-card-title">Learning</h3>
    <p class="ws-card-body">A soft, weighted, decaying <strong>preference</strong> — what you like.
      "Negatives in parentheses", "warm palette, not green", "square corners." Retrieved by
      relevance and applied as taste.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="ws-card">
    <div class="ws-card-icon">!</div>
    <h3 class="ws-card-title">Issue</h3>
    <p class="ws-card-body">A hard, mandatory <strong>rule</strong> the skill must never repeat — an
      explicit "always / never." Not subject to decay; treated as a constraint, not a suggestion.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

A correction becomes a *learning* when it's taste, and an *issue* when it's an "always/never" or a
mistake to never repeat. `capture` classifies and words it; `revise` can `promote` a preference into
a rule or `demote` a rule back to a preference later.

## Weight, decay, and recurrence

Learnings carry a **weight** that captures how strongly a preference is held. Repeating a correction
(`revise … reinforce`) raises it; contradicting one (`weaken`) lowers it; unused learnings **decay**
over time so stale taste fades instead of accumulating forever. This trajectory is exactly what the
**[Metrics → value-over-time](metrics.qmd)** view plots. Issues are mandatory and don't decay.

## Scopes

Entries are grouped by **scope** — a short slug describing *what* the preference is about (e.g.
`currency-formatting`, `color-palette`). Scoping is what makes retrieval precise: `recall` matches
your elaborated intent against scopes, so a table-styling task surfaces table-styling preferences and
nothing else. It's also why passing a rich, elaborated `intent` to `recall` matters so much.

## The learned global layer {#global-layer}

Some preferences aren't about one skill — *"muted palettes, never neon"* is taste you hold whether
you're making a table, a slide, or a web page. Whetstone keeps a reserved, cross-skill store (the
**global layer**) for exactly these.

It changes `recall` by **orchestration only, never by rewriting retrieval**: `recall` runs the *same*
scope-matching it already does against your skill's store, and then runs it a second time against the
global store, and returns the union. Every entry is tagged with an `origin` — `"skill"` or
`"global"` — so when a broad global preference and a specific skill preference disagree, the model has
what it needs to prefer the specific one. Turn the layer off entirely with `consult_global = false`
in config, and `recall` returns a byte-identical per-skill result.

Preferences reach the global layer two ways, both deliberate: `whetstone promote <skill> <id>` lifts
one by hand, and `whetstone compact --all` promotes a preference automatically once it recurs across
enough distinct skills (retiring the per-skill copies). Whetstone **cannot** write your host's memory
(CLAUDE.md, Cursor rules, …) — it is host-agnostic — so this learned, weighted, relevance-retrieved
layer is its honest home for cross-skill taste. It coexists with authored host memory rather than
replacing it.

## Maintenance: compaction & behavioral mining {#maintenance}

Stores stay healthy on their own, but `whetstone compact <skill>` is the periodic tidy-up — run it by
hand or on a schedule, never mid-task. It has two passes:

- A **structural** pass (auto-applied): collapse near-duplicate entries, merge overlapping scopes,
  and retire learnings whose weight has decayed below threshold. Issues are never auto-retired.
- A **behavioral mining** pass (**advisory only**): reading the event log, it flags learnings that
  have earned promotion (`harden`), scopes with capture churn (`bad_capture`), learnings that have
  gone unused (`stale`), and unresolved conflicts (`conflict_residue`). These are *reported* — printed
  and written to a git-ignored `compact-report.md` — and **never applied automatically**; you enact
  one with a `revise`. See **[Tools → compact](tools.qmd#the-out-of-band-cli-not-tools)**.

The split is the whole point: only safe, mechanical cleanup mutates on its own; anything that changes
the *meaning* of your store (promoting a preference to a rule, retiring one you still use) stays your
call.

## Preference packs {#packs}

Because a store is just markdown, your taste is portable. `whetstone export <skill>` writes a
**preference pack** — a `.tar.gz` of the `learnings/` + `issues/` markdown and a `pack.toml` manifest
(private telemetry, the derived index, and git history are left out) — and `whetstone import <skill>
<pack>` folds it into a store. Import is dedup- and conflict-aware (it reuses the exact `capture`
logic) and always **re-mints ids**, so importing a teammate's pack can never collide with your own
entries. It's the friendly, safe path for sharing a house style; because each store is already a git
repo, power users can also just `git remote` and pull.

## Storage & config {#storage-config}

Each skill's learned layer is its **own git repository** under the XDG data dir (default
`~/.local/share/whetstone/<skill-slug>/`; override with `WHETSTONE_STORE_ROOT` or `store_root` in
config):

```default
<store-root>/<skill-slug>/
  learnings/<scope-slug>.md   your preferences, grouped by scope (source of truth)
  issues/<scope-slug>.md      hard rules, grouped by scope (source of truth)
  next_ids.json               per-store id counters (git-tracked; prevents id reuse)
  index.sqlite                derived embedding cache (rebuildable, git-ignored)
  events.jsonl                per-run telemetry for metrics (git-ignored)
  compact-report.md           latest advisory mining findings (git-ignored)
  .git/                       full version history of the markdown
<store-root>/__global__/      the cross-skill learned layer — same structure, its own git repo
```

The markdown is the **source of truth** — read it, edit it, `git revert` it. The SQLite index, the
event log, and the compaction report are derived and git-ignored. The reserved `__global__` store
holds the cross-skill [learned global layer](#global-layer); it is a normal store you can read and
edit like any other. Nothing leaves your machine.

Configuration is read from `~/.config/whetstone/config.toml`, and every key also has a
`WHETSTONE_*` environment override. The most common one is the recall backend:

```toml
# ~/.config/whetstone/config.toml
embedding_backend = "sentence-transformers"   # default: "hashing" (deterministic, dependency-free)
consult_global    = true                       # default true; false = pure per-skill recall
```

The default `hashing` backend needs no extra dependencies and no network. The
`sentence-transformers` backend (install the `embeddings` extra — see **[Install](install.qmd)**)
gives higher-quality, intent-aware retrieval; it's the backend this site's showcase runs on.
